Inguinal herniation

One small sham-controlled trial found lower postoperative pain and better six-month scar scores after 830-nm near-infrared PBM. The study did not assess hernia recurrence.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One small sham-controlled trial found lower postoperative pain and better six-month scar scores after 830-nm near-infrared PBM. The study did not assess hernia recurrence.

Summary of the Evidence

One randomized, single-blind, sham-controlled trial studied 28 people after inguinal-hernia surgery. It measured postoperative pain and scar appearance through six months. No duplicate report, animal study, or cell-culture study was identified for this exact indication. The results concern healing of the incision, not whether the hernia repair remains intact.

Human and clinical evidence

Compared with sham treatment, PBM was associated with lower pain scores and better Vancouver Scar Scale totals at six months. Treated scars were thinner and more pliable on the reported measurements. These are favorable outcomes for postoperative discomfort and scar quality in the studied group (Carvalho et al. 2010). The trial did not measure recurrence of the hernia or establish the rate of keloids in a broader population.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM after inguinal-hernia repair was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly addressing this indication was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used an 830-nm near-infrared GaAlAs laser at 40 mW and 13 J/cm². Each point received 26 seconds of exposure, with ten points along the scar. Four sessions were delivered over seven days. The trial did not compare other wavelengths, doses, or schedules. Its postoperative skin-scar results do not establish outcomes for other hernia operations or for treatment of the hernia itself.

Interpretation

The sham-controlled trial found lower pain and better scar measurements in the treated group at six months. This is a clinically relevant signal from one small study. It supports further testing of incision healing after hernia surgery, but does not establish reduced hernia recurrence or broad prevention of abnormal scars.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for less postoperative pain and improved six-month scar scores after hernia repair
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One sham-controlled randomized study of 28 patients found lower pain and better scar thickness, flexibility, and overall scores at six months. Randomization and sham treatment make the comparison useful, but the estimate comes from a small single trial with no independent replication. A larger trial with blinded scar scoring, pain, recurrence, and adverse-event follow-up would strengthen confidence.
